newsitem.title: UK: Italy rate cut targets 1,000/DM ERM rate-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Italy rate cut targets 1,000/DM ERM rate-analysts.

text.p: The Bank of Italy's decision to lop 75 basis points off official interest rates sooner rather than later has hardened the idea in the market that it wants an ERM central rate of 1,000 per mark or more, analysts said.
"Cutting rates now is a good signal that the last thing Italy wants is a central rate below 1,000," said Tony Norfield, treasury economist at ABN-Amro.
The rate cut was sprung on the market late on Wednesday, pushing mark/lira up four big figures to 1007.00, with the government saying it was just reward for economic rigour.
Italy needs to get the lira back into the exchange rate mechanism (ERM) by the year end in order to have a chance of qualifying for EU economic and monetary union (EMU).
Some see the lira going in at an even more competitive rate.
"The best level for the lira is a slightly weaker level than at the moment. We envisage ERM entry at 1025/1030 or weaker than that," said Sharde Persaud, economist at San Paolo Bank.

Rate cuts are clearly needed to shrink the deficit and get growth going in order to help meet the Maastricht criteria, but with the mark so firm and the lira very much propped up by its yield, a cosy and trouble free ERM entry might be difficult.

The bugbear to a weaker rather than firmer central rate will be Italy's European partners, particularly France, who are unhappy with the competitive edge Italy has gained via a weaker currency since the lira was ejected from the ERM in 1992.

Early this month French President Jacques Chirac said "(It is) quite obvious that the lira's movement is completely incompatible with a single European market, even if it has rebounded slightly recently."
The comment was later dismissed as a "misunderstanding" but analysts said it is obvious France would be happier with a firmer rather than weaker lira to help their own exporters.

"Italy is running out of road," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy. "If they want to get the lira back into the ERM by the end of the year by cutting now they have the option of another cut later this year with the added bonus of reining in the lira."

Looking back to Britain's experience when rates were cut after entry and sterling ended up being flushed out of the ERM, it is better to cut rates before so the currency takes the strain outside the system.

Much to the distress of Italian exporters the lira has rallied strongly in recent weeks -- nearly five percent at one point since early August -- and the Bank of Italy was taking the opportunity to buy cheap marks.
The effect of this was two-fold. Not only did it hold back the lira but it also added to the Bank of Italy's war-chest, should marks be needed to prop up the lira once it joins the ERM.

If the lira joins with a 1,000 per mark central rate and 15 percent bands, the top end would be around 1,150 and the bottom 850 but the ghost of 2.25 percent bands would stand around 1,023 and 977, levels which the volatile lira could easily test.
"It's still all the rage among those in the ERM and those wanting to join to shadow the old 2.25 percent bands," ABN's Norfield said.
"In the lira's case it's more likely the top end of the mark/lira range will be tested given mark strength and they may have to offload some of that war-chest rather sooner than they thought."
